subtitle.en: Eight weeks: money, marks and wellbeing

blurb.en: The core rehearsal: lecture shock, Societies Day, a late allowance, family requests, test week and the Semester Forecast. About 10 minutes.

text.en: Your first big tests. Your results depend on the choices you made in earlier weeks.

label.en: Talked it through with a friend
No laptop and no lab time
A team or society to lean on

text.en: The lecturer says "you did this in high school" and moves on. You didn't, and you're embarrassed to ask in English in front of 300 people.

outcome.en: Your voice shakes, but the lecturer explains it again. Three people thank you afterwards.

tip.en: If you're lost, so is half the room. One question helps everyone.

outcome.en: The lecturer shows you where to catch up and tells you about consultation hours.

label.en: Ask a friend in your language

outcome.en: Your friend explains it in your home language and it clicks. You agree to compare notes every week.

tip.en: Nobody to ask yet? Start in the class WhatsApp group, or ask your tutor to pair you with a study partner.

outcome.en: You nod along and copy the slides. The gap grows a little with every lecture.

tip.en: Not knowing school content isn't a failing. Schools cover different things, and lecturers expect questions.

text.en: In class, your {mod1} lecturer says you need the prescribed textbook for the assignments. It costs R900 at the campus bookshop. You have {money}.

events.research: Understanding Students Issue 2: many skip materials due to cost

outcome.en: You have the book on day one. That was most of a month's food money.
You rely on the slides. The assignment questions come straight from chapters you can't see.
The library has a free e-book version and two copies on short-loan, and a classmate shares theirs before tests. It costs nothing.

tip.en: Search the library catalogue for a free e-book version, and ask your lecturer whether an open textbook or an older edition will do. The help desk keeps prescribed books on short-loan.

outcome.en: A second-year sells you their copy for R250, with their notes still in the margins.

tip.en: For second-hand copies, ask in your class or faculty WhatsApp group, or at the SRC book exchange. Check that it is the right edition.

text.en: Campus is full of stalls. A sports team is recruiting, your friends are signing a gym contract (R300 a month by debit order), the student gym costs R80, and dozens of societies want you.

outcome.en: You pay a small membership fee and meet people at the first practice. Your week has a new anchor.

tip.en: Clubs and societies are one of the cheapest ways to make friends and feel at home.

outcome.en: Training with friends feels great. R300 now leaves your account every month, whether you go or not.

tip.en: Debit orders are easy to sign and hard to stop. Add them up before you commit.

outcome.en: The campus gym is R80 a month with no contract. You go twice a week with a neighbour.

tip.en: Ask what the student option costs before you sign an outside contract.

outcome.en: You head back to your room. It's quieter and cheaper, but you don't know many people yet.

tip.en: You don't have to join much. One group, even a small one, makes the semester less lonely.

outcome.en: You tell the stall you can't afford it. They point you to societies that are free to join, and you sign up for one.

tip.en: Many societies are free. Ask before you assume you can't join.

events.research: Understanding Students Issue 2: cost stops many students joining

text.en: The person who usually helps at home can't come this week, and it is the same morning as your {mod1} tutorial. Tutorials count towards your marks.

outcome.en: Home is covered, but you lose the tutorial mark and the worked answers.

tip.en: Most departments let you move to another tutorial group if you ask early.

label.en: Email the tutor about another group

outcome.en: The tutor moves you to the Thursday afternoon group for good. Students with jobs and children ask this all the time.

label.en: Ask a classmate for the notes

outcome.en: A classmate sends photos of the notes and the answers. You return the favour the next week.

text.en: It's Wednesday night and your {mod1} quiz closes at midnight. The Wi-Fi at your place isn't working, and your data has just run out. A 500 MB bundle costs R49. You have {money}.

outcome.en: You finish the quiz. Data is now one of your biggest weekly costs.

tip.en: Data adds up fast. Know where free Wi-Fi is before you need it.

outcome.en: Your friend shares data and you submit with two minutes to spare.

tip.en: Friends help. A plan for data helps more.

label.en: Use a campus lab or Wi-Fi

outcome.en: A lab is open late. You finish the quiz and learn that campus Wi-Fi is free for students.

tip.en: Campus Wi-Fi and computer labs can save you hundreds a month on data.

title.en: A new friend from your team

text.en: After practice, a teammate invites you for vetkoek. By the end of the night you have a running joke and a study buddy.
It's week three. NSFAS allowances for your group still haven't been paid and you have {money} left. Food is running out.

outcome.en: You eat this week. You'll pay your friend back when the allowance lands.

tip.en: Borrowing works short-term. Write down who you owe and repay on payday.

label.en: Skip meals to make it stretch

outcome.en: You get by on bread and tea. It's hard to concentrate in lectures.

tip.en: Hunger hits your marks too. Food support exists so you don't have to do this.

label.en: Skipping meals caught up with you

outcome.en: The food programme gives you a parcel and vouchers, and financial aid checks on your payment.

tip.en: Most South African universities run food support. Ask student affairs what yours offers.

text.en: It's week three. Your bursary stipend still hasn't been paid and you have {money} left. Food is running out.

title.en: The money from home is late

text.en: It's week three. The money from home hasn't come yet this month and you have {money} left. Food is running out.
It's week three. Your first pay or loan payment still hasn't come through and you have {money} left. Food is running out.
Someone at home calls. The electricity has run out and they need {amount} until month-end. You have {money}.

outcome.en: Home is grateful. Your own month gets tight: food for the last week is uncertain.

tip.en: Helping home matters. Budgeting for it upfront makes it sustainable.

outcome.en: You send {half} and explain what you can manage. It helps, and you still eat.

tip.en: Sending part and being clear about your limits is a real option.

outcome.en: It's a hard conversation. They understand more than you expected, and you agree to plan together next month.

tip.en: Saying "not this month" is allowed. Planning together beats guessing.

title.en: Your tutor notices you've gone quiet

text.en: You've missed two {mod1} tutorials, and the {mod2} assignment is due soon. Your tutor messages: "Haven't seen you in a while. Everything okay?"

outcome.en: The message sits there. So does the work you missed.

tip.en: Tutors reach out because falling behind is common and fixable. Replying is the first step.

label.en: Say you're fine, catch up alone

outcome.en: You catch up on most of it through two late nights. You're exhausted.

tip.en: Saying "I'm fine" when you're not makes the next weeks harder.

label.en: Admit you're struggling and meet them

outcome.en: Your tutor walks you through what you missed and books you a session with an academic coach.

tip.en: One honest reply turned a slide into a plan.

title.en: {mod1} test and {mod2} assignment in the same week

text.en: Your {mod1} test is on Thursday and the {mod2} assignment is due Friday. It's Monday, and you haven't started either.

textAppend.en: Without a laptop, you'll need a campus computer for the assignment.

outcome.en: You hand in both, barely awake. The work is rushed.

tip.en: All-nighters get things done but cost you later.

outcome.en: Without a laptop you can't work through the night at home. You type the assignment on your phone and it shows.

label.en: Drop the assignment for the test

outcome.en: The test goes okay. The zero for {mod2} will hurt your semester mark.

tip.en: A missed assignment is a hole that's hard to climb out of.

outcome.en: An academic coach helps you split the week into blocks: test topics first, assignment in two sittings. You finish both, and sleep.

tip.en: Clashing deadlines are predictable. Put every due date in one calendar in week one.

outcome.en: A coach helps you plan the week around computer-lab hours. You finish both, and sleep.

events.research: Understanding Students Issue 2: workload and time management

title.en: Lonely, can't sleep, thinking of going home

text.en: Everyone else seems to have found their people. You lie awake missing home, and you've started looking at bus tickets. This is one of the most common feelings in first year, and it does pass with support.

outcome.en: You keep going, but the nights are long. It's okay to ask for help at any point.

tip.en: Homesickness is easier with people around you.

outcome.en: Familiar voices help. Your family tells you they're proud of you, and you sleep a little better.

tip.en: Home is support too. On campus, a mentor or society can add to it.

outcome.en: A counsellor helps with sleep and homesickness, and a mentor invites you to a society meetup that week.

tip.en: Feeling lonely in first year is common, and support is free.

title.en: You can't sleep, and you're thinking of quitting

text.en: Everything feels heavy. You lie awake going over money and marks, and you've started wondering whether university is for you. Lots of first-years feel this way, and it does pass with support.

outcome.en: You keep going, but you're running on empty. It's okay to ask for help at any point.

tip.en: Pushing through alone is harder than it needs to be.

outcome.en: Your friend admits they feel the same. Just saying it out loud helps.

tip.en: You're not the only one. Friends help, and counsellors can help more.

outcome.en: A counsellor sees you that week. It's free and confidential, and you leave with a plan for sleep and stress.

tip.en: Counselling is free, confidential and for exactly this.

text.en: Your first big tests. Your results depend on the choices you made in earlier weeks.
{best}: {bestScore}%. You screenshot it before you've even finished reading.
Your {worst} mark is {worstScore}%. At school you were near the top of the class. Lots of first-years have this moment, and it isn't a verdict on you.

events.research: Understanding Students Issue 1: the freshman myth

outcome.en: You stop going to its lectures. The exam is still coming.
You go through the paper line by line. Most lost marks were in one topic, and that's fixable.

tip.en: You can ask to see your marked script. The module guide gives the viewing time, or email the lecturer.

outcome.en: A coach shows you how university tests are marked differently from school. Your next mark goes up.

text.en: Here's where your semester landed, and why it matters for second year.

title.en: Rent is late, and the Wi-Fi is off

text.en: Your funder hasn't paid this month's rent. The landlord has switched off the Wi-Fi and says you have until Friday.

outcome.en: The Wi-Fi stays off for two weeks. You do assignments on campus and avoid the landlord.
You send the landlord proof that your funding is approved. He turns the Wi-Fi back on and agrees to wait.

tip.en: Ask the financial aid office or your funder for a funding confirmation letter, and attach it to your message.

label.en: Ask financial aid for a letter

outcome.en: Financial aid gives you a letter confirming that payment is on its way. The landlord backs off.

tip.en: Tell your landlord early, in writing, and ask your funder for a confirmation letter.

title.en: "Cheap room near campus, pay the deposit today"

text.en: A post offers a room five minutes from campus for half the usual price. The "landlord" says three others are interested: pay R1 500 today to secure it.

outcome.en: The number stops answering, and the room never existed. This happens to students every year, and it's not your fault.

tip.en: Never pay a deposit for a room you haven't seen, with a lease you haven't signed.

outcome.en: The "landlord" makes excuses and can't show you the room. You walk away: good instinct.

tip.en: A real landlord will always let you view the room.

outcome.en: It's not on {short}'s accredited list, and the same photos appear on a listing in another city. You report the post.

tip.en: Check accreditation and search the photos before paying anything.

title.en: The commute is wearing you down

text.en: Two taxis each way: four hours a day on the road. You get home at 8pm too tired to study, and fares have just gone up.

outcome.en: You're exhausted by Thursday and the late starts keep adding up.

tip.en: Commuting time is study time lost. Plan around it.

outcome.en: You study in the library until the rush is over, and travel back with classmates.

tip.en: Use campus time well and travel with others for safety.

outcome.en: You find the support set up for commuting students, with study space and a community on campus.

tip.en: Commuting students have support too. Find your people on campus.

title.en: The gym debit order you forgot about

text.en: You haven't been to the gym in three weeks. The R300 still left your account this month.

outcome.en: Next week becomes the week after.
There's a one-month notice fee, then the debit order stops for good.

tip.en: Cancel in writing, keep the reference number, and check your next bank statement to see that it stopped.

outcome.en: Three mornings a week with friends. Now it's worth the money.

title.en: Your floor goes out every night

text.en: Res life is fun. Your floor heads out most nights, and someone is always playing music at 2am. Your {mod1} tutorials are at 7:30.

outcome.en: Great memories, but you sleep through two tutorials.

tip.en: Fun matters. So does sleep before early classes.

outcome.en: You keep your friends and your mornings.

tip.en: Simple rules, like weekends only, protect your week.

outcome.en: The house committee sets quiet hours and points you to the res study room and peer mentors.

tip.en: Res has structures to help. Use them.

text.en: It's 7pm and already dark when your study group, lab or late lecture ends. Your room or your taxi rank is a twenty-minute walk away.

outcome.en: You make it back, heart pounding. You don't want to do that every week.
Four of you go the same way. You start a "walk home" group chat.

tip.en: Ask in the class WhatsApp group who walks your way. Stick to lit, busy routes even when a shortcut is quicker.

outcome.en: You follow the marked safe route, and security walks you the last stretch. You save their number.

title.en: A lecture on the other campus

text.en: One of your modules is taught on Main Campus at 8am. The inter-campus shuttle leaves your gate at 7:15, and the next one gets there too late.

outcome.en: You pay R40 and still walk in fifteen minutes late. This will happen every week.
It's an early start, but it's free and you get the front row. You save the timetable on your phone.
The faculty office shows you the shuttle timetable and tells you the lecture is recorded for days you can't make it.

tip.en: Ask your faculty office for the shuttle timetable in week one, and check which services are only on Main Campus.

title.en: Water and power cut in your building

text.en: No water since this morning, and now the power's gone too. Your notes are on a phone at 30%.

outcome.en: The library has backup power and working taps. You stay until closing.
It comes back at midnight. The evening is gone.
Their area still has power. You cook together and study after.

text.en: Your friend says a tutor keeps ignoring her questions and joked about "people like her". She believes it's about her race, and wants to switch groups.

label.en: Tell her to let it go

outcome.en: She switches groups quietly. It keeps happening to other students.
She feels less alone, and you go to the next tutorial together.
You find the office that handles discrimination complaints. She decides to report, with you there.

title.en: An international friend faces xenophobic comments

text.en: Your friend from another country is struggling to adjust, and someone in your res made xenophobic comments about them.

outcome.en: They eat alone more often after that.
They join your Friday group. They cook the best food anyone has tasted all term.
The international students office has a peer group, and the comments get reported.

title.en: A friend seems shaken after a party

text.en: A friend tells you that something happened to her at a party last weekend, and that she hasn't told anyone else.

outcome.en: She goes quiet. Being heard matters, and it's never too late to offer support.
She cries, then breathes. You don't need the right words, only to be there.
You find the 24-hour helpline and campus health together. She decides what happens next.

text.en: You met someone in the library queue and now you're texting at 2am about nothing. Your data and your sleep are suffering.

outcome.en: Best two weeks of the term. Your {mod2} lecturer no longer recognises you.
Wednesday date night, weekends for study. Romance with a timetable.
They say they'll wait. They probably won't, and that's okay too.

title.en: A friend thinks she might be pregnant

text.en: Your friend tells you she might be pregnant. She's scared, and she doesn't know who else to tell.

outcome.en: She smiles, but she's still carrying it alone.

label.en: Go with her to campus health

outcome.en: Campus health is free and confidential. Whatever the result, she knows her options now.

label.en: Help her talk to a counsellor

outcome.en: A counsellor talks her through every option, at her pace.

title.en: A friend comes out to you

text.en: Your friend tells you they're gay, and that you're the first person at university they've told.

outcome.en: They go quiet. It took a lot to tell you.
They laugh with relief. Nothing changes between you, except that you're closer.
There's a campus society for LGBTQI+ students and allies. They walk in nervous and walk out laughing.

text.en: Your friend is running the society's movie night now, and they introduce you to everyone.

title.en: A loan shark offers quick cash

text.en: You have skipped meals for days, and the allowance still hasn't come. Someone in your area lends money "no questions asked": R600 now, R900 back at month-end. You have {money}.

outcome.en: The cash helps today. In two weeks R900 leaves your pocket: R300 extra for a two-week loan.

tip.en: Informal loans can cost far more than they look. Always ask what the total repayment is.

label.en: Paid back the loan shark: R900

outcome.en: It's an awkward call, but they help with R300 and no interest.

tip.en: Borrowing from people you trust is cheaper and safer than a loan shark.

label.en: Paid back your loan from home

outcome.en: The financial aid office checks whether you qualify for emergency support, and campus food support covers the rest of the month.

tip.en: Universities have emergency support for exactly this. Ask before you borrow.

text.en: Your class has a WhatsApp group for notes, test dates and venue changes.

outcome.en: Now you hear about venue changes before they happen.
You hear about the new test date in the corridor.

text.en: Your friends are heading to KFC. That's R90 you hadn't planned for this week. You have {money}.

outcome.en: Fun night. Thin week.
Two friends were relieved you said it.

text.en: It's 7:15 and raining. Go to the 8am lecture?

outcome.en: Half the class is missing. You get the test hints.
Extra sleep. The slides online don't quite make sense.

text.en: You answer a question in a tutorial, and someone laughs at your accent.

outcome.en: Your answer was right, and the tutor says so.
You say less this week. Your accent was never the problem.

text.en: It's 1am after a night out, and home is twenty minutes away.

outcome.en: You split the fare four ways and message when you're in.
You get home fine, heart pounding. Next time, plan the ride first.

text.en: It's late, you're tired, and the fridge has eggs and bread. Order takeaways for R85? You have {money}.

outcome.en: Hot food in twenty minutes. That was a day of groceries.
Ten minutes, about R6. Not exciting, but done.
